title: All of Us diversity and scale yield context-dependent improvements in polygenic prediction.
data_url: https://zenodo.org/records/21008909 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21008909) — PRS-CS weight files only; individual-level data via All of Us Researcher Workbench (controlled tier) and UK Biobank application

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Zenodo record 21008909 metadata via its application programming interface: title matches the paper, licence CC-BY-4.0, deposited 2026-06-28, exactly 1 file (prscs_weights.tar.gz, 1,522,933,745 bytes = 1.52 GB; gzip footer reports ~2.52 GB uncompressed). A ranged request returned HTTP 206 with valid gzip magic bytes (1f8b0800), so the file is genuinely public and needs no login. Europe PMC: the Nature Genetics version has no PubMed Central identifier and no open full text; I retrieved the preprint full text instead (PMC11326295, 70k characters of text) and grepped it — zero mentions of 'Workbench', 'Zenodo', 'GitHub' or an 'Availability' section. Polygenic Score (PGS) Catalog search by PubMed identifier 42736379 returned 0 scores and 0 publications. The nature.com article page redirects to a login provider, so the published Data Availability statement was not retrievable.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: 245,388 All of Us whole-genome sequences, UK Biobank with ~500,000 participants, combined discovery of up to ~750,000 participants, 32 traits and diseases, held-out ancestrally diverse All of Us test subset, PRS-CS as the main method. The Zenodo description ('posterior SNP effect estimates from PRS-CS for several quantitative and disease traits, organized by phenotype and discovery GWAS') is the only statement of what is inside the tarball; I did not expand it because 1.52 GB exceeds the 50 MB download cap. That All of Us genomic data sits in the Controlled Tier (institutional Data Use and Registration Agreement, identity verification, Responsible Conduct of Research training, billed cloud compute) comes from the All of Us Research Hub support pages, not from the paper.

a1_downloadable.note: KILLER. The data any polygenic-score project needs — individual genomes plus linked health outcomes — is controlled access. All of Us whole-genome sequences are Controlled Tier: the researcher's institution must sign a Data Use and Registration Agreement, the user must pass identity verification and ethics training, and all analysis runs inside a billed cloud workbench; UK Biobank needs a separate application and fee. Per the rules this is an A1 failure. The only public artefact is a 1.52 GB tarball of PRS-CS model weights (verified reachable, CC-BY-4.0), which contains no people and no phenotypes.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: In the public file there is no outcome column at all — it holds per-variant posterior effect sizes, not anyone's height, lipid level or disease status. The labels (phenotypes) live only behind the controlled-access tiers, so for anything downloadable the prediction target would have to be built from scratch, which it cannot be.

a3_inputs_present.note: The model inputs for polygenic prediction are individual genotypes; none are in the public deposit. The tarball carries single-nucleotide-variant identifiers and effect estimates only, so you would still have to obtain a genotype matrix from a controlled source.

a4_units_stated.note: From the paper's description only, not from the file: PRS-CS posterior effects are per-allele weights on the standardised trait scale (log-odds for binary traits). Standard PRS-CS output columns are documented by that tool. I did not open the tarball (over the 50 MB cap).

a5_enough_rows.note: The unit that matters is the labelled person, and zero labelled people are public. If the unit were instead the trait (for a meta-analysis of when multiancestry training helps), there are 32 traits — far under the ~1,500-row bar. The millions of variant rows inside the weights file are not independent labelled examples.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 1.52 GB compressed / ~2.5 GB uncompressed weights; the real working set (245,388 whole genomes plus phenotypes) is terabyte-scale and only usable inside the All of Us cloud workbench
a6_fits_laptop.note: The weights alone would fit a laptop, but they are not a trainable dataset. The actual analysis the paper does cannot leave the controlled cloud environment, and the project rules deprioritise whole-genome-scale resources.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Could not check. The paper says 32 traits; the Zenodo description says only 'several quantitative and disease traits' and gives no file manifest. The tarball exceeds the download cap, so I could not count phenotype directories or variant rows to reconcile the two.

a8_label_provenance.note: The only downloadable numbers are PRS-CS posterior effect estimates — the output of a Bayesian shrinkage model fitted to genome-wide association summary statistics. Training on them would be distilling that model, the textbook circularity case, and the ceiling would be PRS-CS's own accuracy.

existing_models.name: PRS-CS and PRS-CSx (Bayesian polygenic score methods used by this paper itself)
existing_models.score_and_split: This paper reports polygenic score accuracy for 32 traits in a held-out ancestrally diverse All of Us subset; accuracy declines roughly linearly with genetic distance from the discovery study, and that decline is softened by multiancestry training (numbers read from the abstract and preprint text, not recomputed).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Combining biobanks is not universally best: for less polygenic traits, training on All of Us alone beat the All of Us plus UK Biobank meta-analysis in African-ancestry participants. Why that happens, and how to choose the training set per trait, is left open.

integration.partner_dataset: Polygenic Score (PGS) Catalog, the public registry of published score weight files
integration.join_key: variant identifier (rsID) plus genome build, or trait name
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Could not be made to work: comparing this study's weights with catalogued ones still needs individual genotypes and phenotypes to score anybody, and those are controlled access.

controls.positive_control: None available without individual-level data; the usual control (recover a known strong effect such as APOE for lipids or the FTO region for body mass index) needs genotypes and outcomes.
controls.negative_control: Not runnable — label shuffling requires labels, and none are public.
controls.external_validation: Would be UK Biobank or another biobank, each also behind an application.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is available from the public files, because they contain only another model's fitted coefficients and no measured outcome for any person.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a person's genome to predict their height, cholesterol or disease risk, across many ancestry backgrounds.
plain_idea.train_on: Individual whole-genome sequences linked to health records: 245,388 All of Us participants plus ~500,000 UK Biobank participants (numbers from the paper's abstract, not verified by me, and not obtainable without an access application).
plain_idea.predict: A continuous trait value or a disease yes/no, taken from measured clinical values and electronic health records in each biobank.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Genetic risk scores work much worse for people of non-European ancestry, so anything that narrows that gap matters for whether these scores can be used in clinics at all; the project as posed is blocked because the measurements are not public.

more_or_better_data.why: We would have no data at all: the only public file is 1.52 GB of fitted coefficients, with no people, genotypes or outcomes in it.

confidence_score.why: Per-person confidence needs per-person predictions and truths; neither is downloadable.

models_beatable.why: The paper's own 2026 polygenic scores are evaluated on a held-out ancestrally diverse subset, which is an honest split, and we could not even reproduce their numbers without workbench access.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The first condition fails outright — the existing model cannot be run as our baseline, because scoring anybody requires controlled-access genotypes.

ml_idea: The intended project — train and evaluate multiancestry polygenic risk scores on All of Us plus UK Biobank, or test how prediction accuracy decays with genetic distance from the discovery study — is not buildable from public files. The only open deposit (CC-BY-4.0, 1.52 GB) is PRS-CS posterior variant weights, which are another model's output and carry no phenotypes. A fallback meta-analysis over the 32 traits (predicting which traits gain from biobank meta-analysis) has 32 rows and is a comment, not a model.

effort.compute_note: Only the 1.52 GB compressed weights file (≈2.5 GB uncompressed per its gzip footer) is sizeable and public; I did not expand it because it exceeds the 50 MB cap. No compute estimate is meaningful because there is no trainable table.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open the data availability path and ask whether any individual-level genotype or phenotype can be downloaded without an application. Answer: no — All of Us genomes are Controlled Tier and UK Biobank needs an application. That check took minutes and killed it.

verdict_reason: A1 killer: the genomes and health outcomes are controlled access (All of Us Controlled Tier needs an institutional agreement, identity verification and billed cloud compute; UK Biobank needs an application). The one public deposit, verified reachable at 1.52 GB under CC-BY-4.0, holds only PRS-CS posterior variant weights — another model's output (A8 circularity) with no outcome column (A2) and no genotypes (A3). A trait-level fallback analysis would have 32 rows (A5).
